dedupe_keys.name: hurricanes harvey michael and isaias benchmarking probabilistic and machine learning power outage models across 1 910 us cities

description: This study reviews published statistical and machine learning models that predict hurricane power outages and retrains and tests them on outages across many regions and storms, to see how well they transfer. Prateek Arora and Luis Ceferino of New York University published it in Natural Hazards and Earth System Sciences in May 2023. The data cover hurricanes Harvey in 2017, Michael in 2018 and Isaias in 2020 in 1,910 US cities, with outages from 39 utilities in Texas, 5 in Florida, 5 in New Jersey and 11 in New York, plus land cover, precipitation, soil moisture, tree cover and elevation inputs. State-of-the-art models could not make bounded predictions, overpredicted outages in cities with few outages by an average ratio of 5.2, and did not capture the spread of outages at winds above 70 metres per second. Coverage is four US states. Format and access: open article with a supplement; input sources are listed, and no model code link was given. Licence: CC-BY-4.0; free. Caveats: outage counts come from a commercial aggregator. It is a benchmark for hazard exposure and resilience models of hurricane damage to power grids. Related catalogue records are the PowerOutage.com outage data products and the FMI storm outage prediction model.
